abdominal-brace.name: Learning to brace (do this first)
abdominal-brace.purpose: Every core exercise on this sheet depends on this one skill: stiffening the trunk without holding your breath and without flattening your back into the floor.
abdominal-brace.dose: 10 × 10-second braces, once or twice a day for the first week
how_to: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Put your fingertips on the muscles just inside your hip bones.

Imagine someone is about to poke you in the stomach, and stiffen your whole abdominal wall against it — a firm, all-round tension, about 20–30% of your maximum. You should feel the muscles under your fingers tighten.
Do **not** suck your stomach in, and do **not** push your low back flat against the floor. The natural small hollow in your low back should stay.
Keep breathing normally while you hold it. Say your address out loud to prove you are not holding your breath.
Hold 10 seconds, relax 5 seconds, repeat 10 times.
abdominal-brace.progression: Practise bracing while sitting, standing, and while getting out of a chair — this is where it actually protects you.
abdominal-brace.regression: If you cannot brace and breathe at the same time, drop the effort to 10% and just practise the breathing.
abdominal-brace.safety: Breath-holding raises blood pressure. If you have heart disease or aneurysm, keep the effort light and the breathing continuous.
abdominal-brace.evidence_note: Bracing (all-round stiffening) rather than hollowing (drawing the belly in) is what generates spine stability under real-world loads. The two approaches have been argued over for twenty years; bracing is the more robust skill for daily activity.

mcgill-curl-up.name: Modified curl-up
mcgill-curl-up.purpose: Trains the front of the trunk without repeatedly bending the spine — which is the entire reason we do not use sit-ups.
mcgill-curl-up.dose: Hold 10 seconds; 6 reps, then 4, then 2 (rest ~20 s between sets)
how_to: Lie on your back. Bend **one** knee with that foot flat on the floor; leave the other leg straight.
Slide both hands, palms down, under the small of your back to support its natural hollow. Do not let your back flatten onto your hands.
Brace your abdominal wall as you practised.

Lift your head and shoulders only a centimetre or two off the floor — the head and neck ride with the chest as one rigid unit, as if head, neck and upper chest were in a plaster cast. Your chin does not tuck to your chest and your low back does not move.
Hold for 10 seconds, breathing normally, then lower.
Do 6 holds, rest, 4 holds, rest, 2 holds. Swap which knee is bent halfway through your sets.
mcgill-curl-up.progression: Once 6-4-2 is easy, add a set (8-6-4), or lift the elbows a centimetre off the floor during the hold.
mcgill-curl-up.regression: Do not lift the head at all — simply brace and press the head lightly back into the floor for 10 seconds.
mcgill-curl-up.safety: If you get neck pain, you are lifting with your neck instead of your trunk. Lift less, and think of the whole upper body rising as one block.
mcgill-curl-up.evidence_note: Short 8–10 second holds in a descending pyramid build the muscular *endurance* that distinguishes healthy backs from painful ones, without the repeated flexion cycles that damage discs in laboratory testing.

side-bridge.name: Side bridge (side plank)
side-bridge.purpose: Trains the sides of the trunk — the muscles that stop you collapsing sideways — with very low compressive load on the spine.
side-bridge.dose: Hold 10 seconds; 6 reps, then 4, then 2, each side
how_to: Lie on your side with your knees bent to about 90°, propped on the elbow directly under your shoulder, forearm flat.
Place your top hand on the opposite shoulder.
Brace, then lift your hips off the floor so your body makes a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Hold 10 seconds, breathing normally, then lower.
Do 6, 4, then 2 holds on that side, then roll over and repeat.
side-bridge.progression: Straighten the legs and support on your feet instead of your knees. Then, from the full position, roll slowly forwards and backwards a few degrees while staying stiff.
side-bridge.regression: Keep the hips on the floor and simply hold the propped-up position with a brace. Or do it standing, leaning your forearm on a wall and pushing your hip in towards it.
side-bridge.safety: Painful shoulder is the usual limiter — do the wall version instead. Do not let the bottom shoulder sag.
side-bridge.evidence_note: The side bridge produces high activity in the lateral trunk muscles while keeping spinal compression far lower than sit-ups, which is why it is preferred for painful backs.

bird-dog.name: Bird dog
bird-dog.purpose: Trains the muscles along the back of the spine and teaches you to move an arm and a leg while the spine stays still — the pattern you need for lifting, gardening and vacuuming.
bird-dog.dose: Hold 10 seconds; 6 reps, then 4, then 2, each side
how_to: Kneel on all fours, hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Use a mat or folded towel under the knees.
Brace your abdominal wall and set your back in its natural, neutral position — not arched up, not sagged down.

Slide one arm forward along the floor and the opposite leg back, then lift both just to the height of your body. No higher: hips and shoulders stay square and level, as though balancing a cup of tea on your low back.
Make a fist and reach it away, and push your heel away, as if pushing two walls apart. Hold 10 seconds while breathing.
Return to all fours, sweep the hand and knee under you to touch briefly, then repeat.
Do 6, 4, then 2 holds, then swap sides.
bird-dog.progression: Draw a small square in the air with the raised hand and the raised foot while the trunk stays completely still.
bird-dog.regression: Lift the arm only, then the leg only, before combining them.
bird-dog.safety: Sore wrists — make a fist and rest on your knuckles, or do it with forearms on a bench. Do not lift the leg high enough to arch your back.
bird-dog.evidence_note: Bird dog loads the spinal extensors while keeping the spine in a neutral, low-stress position, which is the recurring principle in every exercise on this page.

dead-bug.name: Dead bug
dead-bug.purpose: Teaches you to keep your low back still while your arms and legs move — the same skill as bird dog, trained lying down where it is easier to control.
how_to: Lie on your back, knees bent up over your hips, arms pointing at the ceiling.
Brace lightly. Your low back keeps its small natural hollow — a hand slid underneath should feel light, steady pressure that does not change.
Slowly lower one arm overhead and straighten the opposite leg towards the floor, going only as far as you can go without the pressure under your back changing.
Breathe out as you extend, and bring them back slowly.
Alternate sides. Stop the set as soon as the low back starts to arch.
dead-bug.progression: Take the leg lower and closer to the floor; slow the movement to a four-second count each way.
dead-bug.regression: Move one limb at a time; keep the moving leg bent and just slide the heel along the floor.
dead-bug.safety: If your back arches or your neck strains, you have gone too far — shorten the range.
dead-bug.evidence_note: Motor-control exercises like this reduce pain and disability in chronic low back pain, though they are not clearly better than other well-delivered exercise. The best programme remains the one you will actually do.

glute-bridge.name: Glute bridge
glute-bridge.purpose: Strengthens the buttock muscles, which take load off the low back when you stand, lift and climb stairs. Weak buttocks means an overworked back.
how_to: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip-width apart, arms by your sides.
Brace gently, then squeeze your buttocks and lift your hips until your body makes a straight line from knees to shoulders.
The lift comes from squeezing the buttocks, not from arching the low back — you should feel it behind, not in the spine.
Hold 5 seconds, then lower slowly.
Repeat 10 times.
glute-bridge.progression: Hold longer (10 seconds), then march slowly on the spot at the top, then do it with one foot lightly off the floor.
glute-bridge.regression: Lift only halfway; or simply squeeze the buttocks hard for 5 seconds without lifting.
glute-bridge.safety: Hamstring cramp is common — move your feet slightly further from your bottom and squeeze the buttocks harder.
glute-bridge.evidence_note: Hip extensor strength is consistently reduced in people with persistent low back pain, and hip strengthening is a standard part of effective back programmes.

front-plank.name: Front plank (optional)
front-plank.purpose: A whole-trunk isometric hold. Useful, but not essential — the Big 3 cover the same ground with less shoulder and back strain.
how_to: Rest on your forearms and knees, elbows under your shoulders.
Brace, and lift your knees so your body makes a straight line from knees or feet to shoulders.
Squeeze your buttocks, and do not let your hips sag or hike up.
Hold 10–20 seconds with normal breathing, then rest. Three holds are plenty.
front-plank.progression: From the knees to the toes; then lift one foot slightly for a few seconds at a time.
front-plank.regression: Do it standing, with your forearms on the kitchen bench and your body angled forwards.
front-plank.safety: Stop the moment your back begins to sag — a sagging plank loads exactly the structures we are protecting.
front-plank.evidence_note: Long plank holds are popular but there is no benefit in grinding out minutes: endurance for daily life is built with repeated short holds, not one exhausting one.

wall-press-antirotation.name: Standing anti-twist press
wall-press-antirotation.purpose: The most useful core work is done standing up. This trains your trunk to resist being twisted — exactly what happens when you carry shopping on one side or open a heavy door.
how_to: Stand about half a metre from a wall, side-on, feet hip-width apart.
Put both hands together, palms flat, against the wall at chest height, arms straight out in front of you.
Brace your trunk, and press your hands into the wall as if trying to push it away. The wall will try to twist you — do not let it.
Keep your hips and shoulders square and your trunk absolutely still. Breathe normally.
Hold 10 seconds, rest, and do five holds before turning around to face the other way.
wall-press-antirotation.progression: Stand in a narrow stance, then in a split stance, then press harder.
wall-press-antirotation.regression: Stand closer to the wall and press more gently.
wall-press-antirotation.safety: Keep breathing. If you feel it in your shoulder rather than your trunk, lower your hands slightly.
wall-press-antirotation.evidence_note: Trunk stiffness generated while standing is what actually protects the spine during daily tasks; floor exercises alone do not automatically transfer.

back-walking.name: Walking as treatment for your back
back-walking.purpose: Regular walking is one of the best-supported treatments for recurrent low back pain, and it is free.
how_to: Start with what you can do comfortably, even if that is ten minutes.
Increase by a few minutes each week rather than doubling it in one go.
Walk at a comfortable, relaxed pace — this is not a fitness test.
Expect some stiffness at first. Movement is safe; the back is a robust structure, and it does better with load than with rest.
If pain flares after a walk, shorten the next one rather than stopping altogether.
back-walking.progression: Longer, then slightly brisker; add gentle hills.
back-walking.regression: Three short walks a day instead of one long one; walk in water if land walking is too painful.
back-walking.safety: Bed rest is the one thing we now know makes back pain worse. Even during a flare, keep moving little and often.
back-walking.evidence_note: An individually tailored, progressive walking programme substantially prolonged the time to a recurrence of low back pain in a large Australian randomised trial (the WalkBack trial, published in The Lancet in 2024).
